# Quantitative centroid-graph control by Brunn--Minkowski surplus

The statements here are bounded continuous and finite-fiber lemmas. They
do not assert a weighted counting-centerpoint theorem for a nonsingleton
centroid graph, and do not remove the unequal-volume gap in OC.

Let d>=1, let K_1,...,K_m be d-dimensional convex bodies of volumes w_i>0,
let lambda_i>0 sum to one, and suppose

    M=sum_i lambda_i K_i subset B,

where B is a d-dimensional convex body of volume b. Put

    x=sum_i lambda_i g_(K_i),
    a=[sum_i lambda_i w_i^(1/d)]^d, delta=1-a/b.

Ordinary Brunn--Minkowski gives 0<a<=b, so 0<=delta<1.

## 1. A dominated measure with the exact weighted centroid

There is a probability coupling pi of the uniform probability laws on
the K_i such that

    eta=a (sum_i lambda_i X_i)#pi <=1_M dx<=1_B dx.   (1)

Its mass is a and its centroid is exactly x. In particular there is a
point z in B such that

    b g_B=a x+(b-a)z                               (2)

when a<b. When a=b, eta=1_B dx and x=g_B.

Proof of the coupling, including nonsmooth bodies. For epsilon>0 convolve
each uniform probability density 1_(K_i)/w_i with the same centered
nondegenerate Gaussian of covariance epsilon^2 Id. The resulting f_i are
smooth strictly positive probabilities bounded above by 1/w_i. Use f_1
as a common reference density f. Match successive conditional cumulative
distribution functions to construct triangular maps T_i pushing f dx to
f_i dx; take T_1=Id. Their diagonal derivatives are positive, and their
Jacobian determinants obey

    det DT_i(t)=f(t)/f_i(T_i(t))>=w_i f(t).           (3)

Here the maps can be constructed recursively. First match the first
marginal CDFs. Having matched the preceding coordinates, match the next
conditional CDF. All conditional densities are smooth and strictly
positive, so each matching map is strictly increasing from minus infinity
to plus infinity, and the implicit function theorem gives smoothness.
Multiplying the conditional density identities gives (3) and the ordinary
change-of-variables identity. Gaussian decay justifies differentiation of
the marginal integrals on every compact set.

The average F=sum lambda_i T_i is again a triangular diffeomorphism with
positive diagonal entries: with previous coordinates fixed, each new
coordinate increases strictly between the two infinite endpoints. If the
diagonal entries of DT_i are c_(ij)>0, Holder's inequality gives

 [det DF]^(1/d)
   =[product_j sum_i lambda_i c_(ij)]^(1/d)
   >=sum_i lambda_i [product_j c_(ij)]^(1/d)
   >=f(t)^(1/d) sum_i lambda_i w_i^(1/d).

The first inequality can also be obtained directly by applying Holder to
the d sequences (lambda_i c_(ij))^(1/d). Thus det DF>=a f(t), and the
pushforward probability density is at most 1/a.

The joint laws of (T_1,...,T_m) under f dx are tight because their finitely
many marginals converge to compactly supported uniform laws. Take a weakly
convergent subsequence. Its limit pi has exactly those uniform marginals.
The averaging map is continuous, so its pushforwards converge weakly. For
each nonnegative compactly supported continuous test function, the density
bound above passes to the limit and gives eta<=dx. The limiting marginals
are supported on the compact K_i, hence eta is supported on their compact
Minkowski average M. This proves (1).

Its moment is computed from the limiting compactly supported coupling:
each marginal has mean g_(K_i), hence eta's mean is x. No convergence of
unbounded moments is used. The nonnegative residual measure 1_B dx-eta
has mass b-a. Its centroid z belongs to B by convexity, proving (2).

Notice that (1) is stronger than a geometric-mean volume bound: its mass
is the full Brunn--Minkowski quantity a. It does not identify x with the
centroid of M, which is generally a different point.

## 2. Exact vector containment and directional shift bounds

Equation (2) and x,z in B imply the exact containments

    x-g_B in [delta/(1-delta)](g_B-B),
    x-g_B in delta(B-B),
    x in B.                                       (4)

Let u be any nonzero linear functional, let

    l=min_B u, h=max_B u, W=h-l>0, c=u(g_B).

Then

 u(x)-c <=min{h-c, delta W,
                         [delta/(1-delta)](c-l)},

 c-u(x) <=min{c-l, delta W,
                         [delta/(1-delta)](h-c)}.   (5)

Every term follows directly from one containment in (4). In particular,

 |u(x-g_B)|/W
 <=min{delta, [d/(d+1)]delta/(1-delta), d/(d+1)}.    (6)

For completeness the centroid support bound used in (6) is elementary.
Normalize the projection of B to [0,1], choose p in B at projection zero,
and observe that tB+(1-t)p is contained in B cap {u<=t}. Thus the uniform
projection CDF is at least t^d. Integrating it gives E[u]<=d/(d+1).
Using the opposite endpoint gives E[u]>=1/(d+1). These are precisely
(c-l)/W,(h-c)/W<=d/(d+1).

There is also a set bound for several representations at the same B.
If each representation has a>= (1-epsilon)b, with 0<=epsilon<1, then
all its weighted centroid points lie in

    B intersect [g_B+(epsilon/(1-epsilon))(g_B-B)].  (7)

Indeed the dilates in (4) are nested since 0 belongs to g_B-B. Therefore
the directional width of the entire set of such points is at most

    [epsilon/(1-epsilon)] W.                       (8)

This is a common containing set, not a sum of two separate distance
estimates. At zero surplus it is exactly the singleton {g_B}.

There is a SHARP directional version for each fixed B and each fixed
ratio a/b. Let c_a be the unique projection threshold for which the upper
cap B_a^+=B cap {u>=c_a} has volume a, and let B_a^- be the analogous
lower cap. For a=b take both caps equal to B. Then

    u(g_(B_a^-))<=u(x)<=u(g_(B_a^+)).                (8a)

To prove the upper bound, subtract volume on B_a^+ from eta. On that cap
the difference has nonpositive density; outside it the difference has
nonnegative density. Hence the integral of (u-c_a) against the difference
is nonpositive. Its total mass is zero, so its u-moment is nonpositive.
Divide by a. The lower inequality is the reversed argument.

In normalized quantile notation, let Q(t) be the upper projection quantile
of uniform B, 0<t<1, and theta=a/b. The exact maximal positive shift is

    [1/theta] integral_0^theta Q(t)dt
                         -integral_0^1 Q(t)dt.    (8b)

Both extrema in (8a) are achieved within the current Minkowski setting:
take every K_i equal to the corresponding cap B_a^+ or B_a^-. They are
also achieved as actual graph points by placing that cap at both integer
indices -1,+1 and B at zero, as in Section 4. Thus (8a) is the exact
directional answer for fixed B and surplus, while (6) supplies a simple
dimension-only estimate with an optimal first-order coefficient.

## 3. A sharp cap consequence of the same representation

For every closed halfspace H containing x,

    |B intersect H|>=gamma_d a,
    gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.                            (9)

One direct proof avoids any assumptions on the shape of eta. If u is the
cap's normal, set A_i=K_i cap {u>=u(g_(K_i))}. Ordinary Grunbaum gives
|A_i|>=gamma_d w_i. Their Minkowski average is contained in
B cap {u>=u(x)}, which is contained in H. Brunn--Minkowski then gives
the right side of (9). All of these are closed caps; their boundaries
have zero d-volume. A halfspace constant on the ambient affine span is
handled by its entire-body trace.

The constant in (9) is sharp for every prescribed a/b in (0,1]. Take B
to be a simplex and let all K_i be one homothetic vertex sub-simplex A
of relative volume a/b. Then x=g_A and the parallel vertex cap through
g_A has B-volume exactly gamma_d a. Thus (9) is an exact cap estimate,
not a claim that the shift estimate (6) is exact at every positive delta.

## 4. First-order sharpness and actual mixed centroid-graph examples

The coefficient d/(d+1) in the small-delta shift bound (6) is optimal.
Normalize B to be a simplex of volume one, with projection X ranging from
zero at one vertex to one on its opposite facet. Its projection density
is d X^(d-1), and its mean is d/(d+1). Remove its vertex cap of volume
delta and set

    A=B cap {X>=delta^(1/d)},  |A|=1-delta.

Its centroid satisfies the exact formula

 g_A[X]-g_B[X]
   =[d/(d+1)] delta(1-delta^(1/d))/(1-delta).        (10)

This follows by integrating d X^d from delta^(1/d) to one and dividing
by 1-delta. Dividing (10) by delta and taking delta down to zero gives
d/(d+1), matching (6) to first order.

This is an actual centroid-graph configuration, not only a nested-body
example. In R x R^d set

    C=conv({-1}xA union {0}xB union {1}xA).

It is a full-dimensional convex body; its integer fibers are exactly
A,B,A, since A subset B. The centroid hull at integer index zero contains
both g_A, from the equal average of the endpoint centroids, and g_B.
The endpoint representation has Brunn--Minkowski mass a=1-delta. Thus
the graph shift in (10) has exactly the surplus delta used in (6).

The width coefficient one in (8) is also optimal to first order, in every
d. Let B=[0,1]xK, where K is any (d-1)-dimensional convex body (for d=1
use just the interval). Let A_left=[0,1-epsilon]xK and
A_right=[epsilon,1]xK. In Z^2 place A_left at both indices +/-e_1,
A_right at both indices +/-e_2, and B at zero, and take their convex hull.
Its projection is the lattice diamond conv{+/-e_1,+/-e_2}, whose only
integer points are these four vertices and zero. The actual central
fiber is B, and the four endpoint fibers are the assigned bodies. The
central centroid graph has projection interval between g_(A_left) and
g_(A_right), of width exactly epsilon. Each of the two endpoint-pair
representations has lower volume a=(1-epsilon)|B|. Formula (8) gives
epsilon/(1-epsilon), so its leading coefficient cannot be reduced.

## 5. Application and intrinsic scope

For positive-volume fibers K_z of a mixed-integer body, let
G=conv{(z,g_z)}. Every point (w,x) of G at an integer index w has a finite
convex representation of this form, with

    B=K_w, a=[sum_z lambda_z |K_z|^(1/d)]^d.

Convexity gives the Minkowski inclusion needed in Section 1. Thus (1)--(9)
apply to every such representation. Multiple representations need not
have the same a; (7) applies to whichever representations meet its stated
volume threshold. At a=b the centroid graph point must equal g_w, even
when the source volumes are unequal.

The same statements hold intrinsically in dimension q when all source
fibers have the maximum dimension q of the mixed intersection and have
positive H_q volume. At an integer output index, the direction space of
their Minkowski sum is the sum of their q-dimensional direction spaces.
Its dimension cannot exceed q, so those spaces coincide, and the output
fiber has that direction space as well. Translate the parallel affine
spans into this common Euclidean q-space and apply the preceding proof
there, with d replaced by q and ordinary volume by H_q. For q=0 all
positive fibers are singleton points and the output is the unique point
of its integer fiber; no transport or zero power is needed.

The estimates control geometric displacement and supply one own-fiber cap
budget. They do not by themselves turn a nonsingleton centroid graph into
a graph with Helly number 2^n, or transfer a weighted counting centerpoint
through all other fibers. That remaining compatibility assertion is not
used anywhere above.
